techniques.name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
techniques.description: RAG evaluation assesses systems combining retrieval and generation by measuring retrieval quality, generation faithfulness, and overall performance. This technique evaluates whether retrieved context is relevant, whether responses faithfully represent information without hallucination, and how systems handle insufficient context. Key metrics include retrieval precision/recall, answer relevance, faithfulness scores, and citation accuracy.

example_use_cases.description: Evaluating a technical support knowledge system at a software company to ensure it retrieves relevant troubleshooting documentation and generates accurate solutions without fabricating configuration steps or commands not present in official documentation.

Assessing whether a legal research assistant properly cites source documents when generating case summaries, enabling lawyers to verify information and trace conclusions back to authoritative sources.

Evaluating a clinical decision support system that retrieves relevant medical literature and patient records to ensure generated treatment recommendations accurately reflect evidence-based guidelines without extrapolating beyond available clinical data.

Assessing a government benefits information chatbot to verify it retrieves relevant policy documents and accurately communicates eligibility criteria without hallucinating benefits, amounts, or requirements that could mislead citizens seeking assistance.

limitations.description: Evaluation requires high-quality ground truth datasets with known correct retrievals and answers, which may be expensive or impossible to create for specialized domains.
Faithfulness assessment can be subjective and difficult to automate, often requiring human judgment to determine whether responses accurately represent retrieved context.
Trade-offs between retrieval precision and recall mean optimizing for one metric may degrade the other, requiring domain-specific balancing decisions.
Metrics may not capture subtle quality issues like incomplete answers, misleading emphasis, or failure to synthesize information from multiple retrieved sources.

Evaluating multi-hop reasoning—where answers require synthesising information across multiple retrieved documents—is particularly challenging, as standard metrics may not capture whether the system correctly chains information or makes unsupported logical leaps.

Difficult to isolate whether poor performance stems from retrieval failures (finding wrong documents), generation failures (misusing correct documents), or interaction effects, complicating diagnosis and improvement efforts.

resources.title: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
resources.abstract: We introduce RAGAs (Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment), a framework for reference-free evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines. RAGAs is available at [https://github.com/explodinggradients/ragas]. RAG systems are composed of a retrieval and an LLM based generation module. They provide LLMs with knowledge from a reference textual database, enabling them to act as a natural language layer between a user and textual databases, thus reducing the risk of hallucinations. Evaluating RAG architectures is challenging due to several dimensions to consider: the ability of the retrieval system to identify relevant and focused context passages, the ability of the LLM to exploit such passages faithfully, and the quality of the generation itself. With RAGAs, we introduce a suite of metrics that can evaluate these different dimensions without relying on ground truth human annotations. We posit that such a framework can contribute crucially to faster evaluation cycles of RAG architectures, which is especially important given the fast adoption of LLMs.

resources.title: Enhancing the Precision and Interpretability of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in Legal Technology: A Survey
resources.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a promising solution that can enhance the capabilities of large language model (LLM) applications in critical domains, including legal technology, by retrieving knowledge from external databases. Implementing RAG pipelines requires careful attention to the techniques and methods implemented in the different stages of the RAG process. However, robust RAG can enhance LLM generation with faithfulness and few hallucinations in responses. In this paper, we discuss the application of RAG in the legal domain. First, we present an overview of the main RAG methods, stages, techniques, and applications in the legal domain. We then briefly discuss the different information retrieval models, processes, and applied methods in current legal RAG solutions. Then, we explain the different quantitative and qualitative evaluation metrics. We also describe several emerging datasets and benchmarks. We then discuss and assess the ethical and privacy considerations for legal RAG and summarize various challenges, and propose a challenge scale based on RAG failure points and control over external knowledge. Finally, we provide insights into promising future research to leverage RAG efficiently and effectively in the legal field.

resources.title: ASTRID - An Automated and Scalable TRIaD for the Evaluation of RAG-based Clinical Question Answering Systems
resources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive potential in clinical question answering (QA), with Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) emerging as a leading approach for ensuring the factual accuracy of model responses.However, current automated RAG metrics perform poorly in clinical and conversational use cases.Using clinical human evaluations of responses is expensive, unscalable, and not conducive to the continuous iterative development of RAG systems.To address these challenges, we introduce ASTRID -an Automated and Scalable TRIaD for evaluating clinical QA systems leveraging RAG -consisting of three metrics: Context Relevance (CR), Refusal Accuracy (RA), and Conversational Faithfulness (CF).Our novel evaluation metric, CF, is designed to better capture the faithfulness of a model's response to the knowledge base without penalizing conversational elements.Additionally, our metric RA captures the refusal to address questions outside of the system's scope of practice.To validate our triad, we curate a dataset of over 200 real-world patient questions posed to an LLM-based QA agent during surgical follow-up for cataract surgery -the highest volume operation in the worldaugmented with clinician-selected questions for emergency, and clinical and non-clinical out-of-domain scenarios.We demonstrate that CF predicts human ratings of faithfulness more accurately than existing definitions in conversational settings.Furthermore, using eight different LLMs, we demonstrate that the three metrics can closely agree with human evaluations, highlighting the potential of these metrics for use in LLM-driven automated evaluation pipelines.Finally, we show that evaluation using our triad of CF, RA, and CR exhibits alignment with clinician assessment for inappropriate, harmful, or unhelpful responses.We also publish the prompts and datasets for these experiments, providing valuable resources for further research and development.

sample_claims.text: The legal research system's generated case summaries are traceable to specific retrieved source documents with verifiable citations
The clinical decision support system generates treatment recommendations that accurately reflect the retrieved evidence-based guidelines without extrapolating beyond available medical literature
The customer support assistant explicitly indicates when retrieved knowledge base articles do not contain sufficient information to answer user queries

techniques.name: Reward Hacking Detection
techniques.description: Reward hacking is when an agent trained to maximise a proxy reward (a reward function or learned reward model that only approximates what its designers want) raises that proxy by exploiting its gaps while the intended outcome stalls or gets worse. Reward hacking detection tests a trained policy for this by scoring it against both the proxy it was optimised for and an independent measure of the intended objective that the optimiser never saw, such as a hand-written true reward in a simulator, a held-out 'gold' reward model or human ratings. The scoring is repeated at every training checkpoint, or across models of increasing size, because the change can be abrupt: the originating study found capability thresholds at which an agent's behaviour shifts and its true reward falls sharply while its proxy reward keeps rising. Where the intended objective cannot be scored in operation, the same study flags a policy as aberrant when its action distribution diverges too far from that of a trusted policy that people have already checked, with the alarm threshold set on policies whose true reward is known. The output is a pair of proxy and true-reward curves showing where they part, or an anomaly score for each candidate policy.

example_use_cases.description: A transport authority training a reinforcement-learning ramp-metering controller in a traffic simulator rewards it on mean vehicle speed, but also logs average commute time for all drivers at every checkpoint. Checkpoints where speed keeps improving while commute time worsens (for example by holding merging cars back indefinitely) are rejected before any field trial.

A team fine-tuning a customer-support language model with reinforcement learning from human feedback scores each checkpoint with its training reward model and with a held-out reward model and a sample of human ratings that the training loop never sees, and stops training at the point where the training reward keeps rising but the held-out scores fall.

Before an insulin-dosing agent trained against a simulator reward goes to clinical evaluation, the developers score every candidate policy on a separate true objective, time spent in the safe blood-glucose range, and exclude any policy whose simulator reward is high but whose time in range is lower than that of the clinically reviewed baseline policy.

A public-health modelling unit that replaces a reviewed epidemic-response policy with a larger retrained one compares the new policy's actions with the reviewed policy's across simulated outbreaks. A divergence score above the threshold set on earlier policies with known outcomes sends the new policy to expert review instead of adoption, because its true outcome cannot be scored before deployment.

limitations.description: Everything rests on the independent measure of the intended objective. When that measure is itself a proxy (a gold reward model, or a small sample of human ratings), a policy can exploit it too, and the comparison then only detects divergence between two imperfect measures. Collecting enough human ratings at every checkpoint is expensive, which is why studies substitute a gold reward model.

It detects gaming only along the dimensions the true measure scores. A policy that exploits something the true objective does not capture (a side effect, a safety constraint, a user group not represented in the ratings) passes the check, so a clean result is evidence about the measured objective only.

The trusted-policy detector is weak and inconsistent. In the originating benchmark every baseline detector scored an area under the ROC curve below 60% on at least one task, and no detector was best on all tasks, so a quiet detector is not evidence that hacking is absent.

The trusted-policy detector flags difference, not harm. It needs a policy that people have already verified, and comparable action distributions from both policies, and a candidate that is genuinely better than the trusted policy can diverge from it and be flagged, which makes false alarms likely when the trusted policy is only moderately good.

Because the onset of reward hacking can be abrupt as capability grows, checking a few checkpoints or one model size can miss it. The comparison has to be repeated at every checkpoint and model size that might be deployed, which multiplies evaluation cost, especially when the true measure needs human raters.

resources.title: The Effects of Reward Misspecification: Mapping and Mitigating Misaligned Models
resources.abstract: Reward hacking -- where RL agents exploit gaps in misspecified reward functions -- has been widely observed, but not yet systematically studied. To understand how reward hacking arises, we construct four RL environments with misspecified rewards. We investigate reward hacking as a function of agent capabilities: model capacity, action space resolution, observation space noise, and training time. More capable agents often exploit reward misspecifications, achieving higher proxy reward and lower true reward than less capable agents. Moreover, we find instances of phase transitions: capability thresholds at which the agent's behavior qualitatively shifts, leading to a sharp decrease in the true reward. Such phase transitions pose challenges to monitoring the safety of ML systems. To address this, we propose an anomaly detection task for aberrant policies and offer several baseline detectors.

resources.title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
resources.abstract: In reinforcement learning from human feedback, it is common to optimize against a reward model trained to predict human preferences. Because the reward model is an imperfect proxy, optimizing its value too much can hinder ground truth performance, in accordance with Goodhart’s law. This effect has been frequently observed, but not carefully measured due to the expense of collecting human preference data. In this work, we use a synthetic setup in which a fixed “gold-standard” reward model plays the role of humans, providing labels used to train a proxy reward model. We study how the gold reward model score changes as we optimize against the proxy reward model using either reinforcement learning or best-of-$n$ sampling. We find that this relationship follows a different functional form depending on the method of optimization, and that in both cases its coefficients scale smoothly with the number of reward model parameters. We also study the effect on this relationship of the size of the reward model dataset, the number of reward model and policy parameters, and the coefficient of the KL penalty added to the reward in the reinforcement learning setup. We explore the implications of these empirical results for theoretical considerations in AI alignment.

techniques.name: Toxicity Detection
techniques.description: Toxicity detection uses automated classifiers and human review to identify harmful, offensive, or dangerous content in model outputs. This technique employs tools trained to detect toxic language, hate speech, threats, and other harmful content through targeted testing with adversarial prompts. Detection covers explicit toxicity (slurs, threats, graphic content) and implicit harm (manipulative advice, dangerous instructions). For bias and fairness evaluation of model outputs, see related techniques such as few-shot fairness evaluation and demographic parity assessment.

example_use_cases.description: Screening a chatbot's responses for toxic language, hate speech, and harmful content before deployment in public-facing applications where vulnerable users including children might interact with it.
Screening an AI writing assistant for educational content to ensure it maintains appropriate language and doesn't generate offensive material that could be harmful in classroom or academic settings.

Screening a mental health support chatbot to ensure it doesn't generate stigmatising language about mental health conditions, substance use, or marginalised communities, which could cause harm to vulnerable patients seeking help.

limitations.description: Toxicity classifiers themselves may have biases, potentially flagging legitimate discussions of sensitive topics or minority language patterns as toxic.
Context-dependent nature of toxicity makes automated detection challenging, as the same phrase may be harmful or harmless depending on usage context.
Evolving language and cultural differences mean toxicity definitions change over time and vary across communities, requiring constant updating.
Sophisticated models may generate subtle bias or coded language that evades automated detection while still being harmful.

Comprehensive toxicity detection often requires human review to validate automated findings and handle edge cases, which is resource-intensive and may not scale to high-volume applications or real-time content generation.

Toxicity classifiers require large labeled datasets of harmful content for training and validation, which are expensive to create, emotionally taxing for annotators, and raise ethical concerns about exposing people to harmful material.

Configuring detection thresholds involves tradeoffs between false positives (over-censoring legitimate content) and false negatives (missing harmful content), with different stakeholders often disagreeing on acceptable balance points.
Detection performance often degrades significantly for non-English languages, code-switching, dialects, and internet slang, limiting effectiveness for global or multilingual applications.

resources.title: RealToxicityPrompts: Evaluating Neural Toxic Degeneration in Language Models
resources.abstract: Pretrained neural language models (LMs) are prone to generating racist, sexist, or otherwise toxic language which hinders their safe deployment.We investigate the extent to which pretrained LMs can be prompted to generate toxic language, and the effectiveness of controllable text generation algorithms at preventing such toxic degeneration.We create and release RE-ALTOXICITYPROMPTS, a dataset of 100K naturally occurring, sentence-level prompts derived from a large corpus of English web text, paired with toxicity scores from a widelyused toxicity classifier.Using REALTOXICI-TYPROMPTS, we find that pretrained LMs can degenerate into toxic text even from seemingly innocuous prompts.We empirically assess several controllable generation methods, and find that while data-or compute-intensive methods (e.g., adaptive pretraining on non-toxic data) are more effective at steering away from toxicity than simpler solutions (e.g., banning "bad" words), no current method is failsafe against neural toxic degeneration.To pinpoint the potential cause of such persistent toxic degeneration, we analyze two web text corpora used to pretrain several LMs (including GPT-2; Radford et al., 2019), and find a significant amount of offensive, factually unreliable, and otherwise toxic content.Our work provides a test bed for evaluating toxic generations by LMs and stresses the need for better data selection processes for pretraining.

resources.title: A New Generation of Perspective API: Efficient Multilingual Character-level Transformers
resources.abstract: On the world wide web, toxic content detectors are a crucial line of defense against potentially hateful and offensive messages. As such, building highly effective classifiers that enable a safer internet is an important research area. Moreover, the web is a highly multilingual, cross-cultural community that develops its own lingo over time. As such, it is crucial to develop models that are effective across a diverse range of languages, usages, and styles. In this paper, we present the fundamentals behind the next version of the Perspective API from Google Jigsaw. At the heart of the approach is a single multilingual token-free Charformer model that is applicable across a range of languages, domains, and tasks. We demonstrate that by forgoing static vocabularies, we gain flexibility across a variety of settings. We additionally outline the techniques employed to make such a byte-level model efficient and feasible for productionization. Through extensive experiments on multilingual toxic comment classification benchmarks derived from real API traffic and evaluation on an array of code-switching, covert toxicity, emoji-based hate, human-readable obfuscation, distribution shift, and bias evaluation settings, we show that our proposed approach outperforms strong baselines. Finally, we present our findings from deploying this system in production.

resources.title: Sample Requests | Perspective API
A Human-centered Evaluation of a Toxicity Detection API: Testing Transferability and Unpacking Latent Attributes
resources.abstract: Perspective is a publicly available, machine learning API that can score text for toxicity. It is available for use in online platforms and communities to limit toxicity and promote civil dialogue. In this work, we adopt a human-centered approach to evaluating Perspective by investigating if human ratings of toxicity align with Perspective’s toxicity scores. We also test its transferability by making this comparison for comments from three platforms that have different commenting styles and moderation strategies: news websites, YouTube, and Twitter. Apart from toxicity, the main attribute, we collect participant ratings for three additional attributes: respectfulness, formality, and presence of stereotypes. While disrespect is part of how Perspective defines toxicity, formality and presence of stereotypes were included in the study to explore if they could be hidden/latent attributes that affect toxicity scores from Perspective. We analyzed how participant ratings for these additional attributes vary with respect to Perspective’s toxicity score for comments from each platform. We find that for high toxicity scores, Perspective strongly aligns with participant ratings of toxicity and disrespectfulness across all three platforms, providing weak evidence of its transferability. However, our evaluation also surfaced formality and presence of stereotypes as latent attributes that are unrecognized parts of Perspective’s scores. We discuss how and why this evaluation is “human-centered,” the importance of conducting such evaluations, and implications of these results for content moderation in social platforms.

resources.title: An Evaluation of the Google Perspective API by Race and Gender
resources.abstract: Research on American politicians demonstrates that minority politicians often face higher rates of uncivil speech online.While previous studies have focused on federal representatives, local politicians engage more frequently with constituents, increasing the risk of online and offline violence.These imminent threats to state-level officials highlight the need for tools that can measure the toxic discourse faced by local politicians, making algorithmic evaluation of these tools essential for understanding these interactions.To this end, this study evaluates the Google Perspective API, a widely used machine learning algorithm that quantifies toxicity.This study assesses the performance of the API across various demographic identities.Using a dataset of one million tweets directed at state legislators across all 50 states in January 2021, I identify significant gender and racial discrepancies in the algorithm's performance.Specifically, the API demonstrates better performance in predicting toxicity toward men than toward women.The racial discrepancies are slightly more nuanced with the API performing better for some races and not others.This research underscores the importance of algorithmic validation and has implications for studies of algorithmic performance, online harassment and political communication.

techniques.name: Isotonic Regression Calibration
techniques.description: Isotonic regression calibration turns a classifier's scores into calibrated probabilities by fitting a step-shaped function that never decreases as the score rises. Unlike a fixed curve, it assumes nothing about the shape of the miscalibration except that a higher score should never mean a lower chance of the positive outcome, so it can correct any distortion that leaves the cases in the right order. It is fitted on labelled cases the classifier was not trained on: the cases are sorted by score, and the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm repeatedly merges neighbouring groups whose observed positive rates are out of order, until the rates rise steadily with the score. Each merged group's observed rate becomes the calibrated probability for scores in its range, and the result is assessed with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and the Brier score (a measure of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened) before and after.

example_use_cases.description: A clinical research team builds a random forest on electronic health records to predict which adolescents will attempt suicide. The forest ranks patients well, but its vote shares are not probabilities, so the team fits isotonic regression on held-out records and reports calibration slope, intercept and Brier score before the risk estimates are used to prioritise clinical follow-up.

An insurer's pricing team applies isotonic recalibration to the output of its claim-probability model, fitted on a large portfolio and checked on a later year of policies, so that within each band of predicted risk the average prediction matches the observed claim rate and no price band systematically subsidises another.

An online marketplace scores listings for fraud with a naive Bayes text classifier whose probabilities cluster near 0 and 1, and analysts had been treating them as near-certainties. With tens of thousands of labelled past cases available, the team fits isotonic calibration so the review queue shows probabilities that match observed fraud rates, and shares the reliability diagram with the analysts.

limitations.description: It needs plenty of calibration data. With fewer than about a thousand labelled cases the step function follows noise in the calibration set. Because each step matches the observed rate exactly on the cases it was fitted to, calibration checked on those same cases looks perfect whatever its true quality, so it must be checked on separate cases. The two-parameter curve of Platt scaling usually does as well or better on small sets; isotonic regression pays off when calibration data are plentiful.

The output is a step function, so many different scores receive exactly the same probability. These ties discard distinctions the model made within a step, can change ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve after calibration, and matter when a decision threshold falls inside a wide step.

It relies on the classifier's ordering being right: a higher score must never mean a lower chance of the outcome. Where the model ranks cases wrongly over some range of scores, isotonic regression cannot repair the ranking and instead flattens that range into a single probability.

Probabilities at the extremes rest on little data. The outermost steps can be fitted from a handful of cases and may sit at or near 0 or 1, and common implementations clip scores beyond the range seen in calibration to the end values, so the most extreme predictions are the least trustworthy.

resources.title: Transforming classifier scores into accurate multiclass probability estimates
resources.abstract: Class membership probability estimates are important for many applications of data mining in which classification outputs are combined with other sources of information for decision-making, such as example-dependent misclassification costs, the outputs of other classifiers, or domain knowledge. Previous calibration methods apply only to two-class problems. Here, we show how to obtain accurate probability estimates for multiclass problems by combining calibrated binary probability estimates. We also propose a new method for obtaining calibrated two-class probability estimates that can be applied to any classifier that produces a ranking of examples. Using naive Bayes and support vector machine classifiers, we give experimental results from a variety of two-class and multiclass domains, including direct marketing, text categorization and digit recognition.

resources.title: Predicting suicide attempts in adolescents with longitudinal clinical data and machine learning
resources.abstract: Background Adolescents have high rates of nonfatal suicide attempts, but clinically practical risk prediction remains a challenge. Screening can be time consuming to implement at scale, if it is done at all. Computational algorithms may predict suicide risk using only routinely collected clinical data. We used a machine learning approach validated on longitudinal clinical data in adults to address this challenge in adolescents. Methods This is a retrospective, longitudinal cohort study. Data were collected from the Vanderbilt Synthetic Derivative from January 1998 to December 2015 and included 974 adolescents with nonfatal suicide attempts and multiple control comparisons: 496 adolescents with other self‐injury ( OSI ), 7,059 adolescents with depressive symptoms, and 25,081 adolescent general hospital controls. Candidate predictors included diagnostic, demographic, medication, and socioeconomic factors. Outcome was determined by multiexpert review of electronic health records. Random forests were validated with optimism adjustment at multiple time points (from 1 week to 2 years). Recalibration was done via isotonic regression. Evaluation metrics included discrimination ( AUC , sensitivity/specificity, precision/recall) and calibration (calibration plots, slope/intercept, Brier score). Results Computational models performed well and did not require face‐to‐face screening. Performance improved as suicide attempts became more imminent. Discrimination was good in comparison with OSI controls ( AUC = 0.83 [0.82–0.84] at 720 days; AUC = 0.85 [0.84–0.87] at 7 days) and depressed controls ( AUC = 0.87 [95% CI 0.85–0.90] at 720 days; 0.90 [0.85–0.94] at 7 days) and best in comparison with general hospital controls ( AUC 0.94 [0.92–0.96] at 720 days; 0.97 [0.95–0.98] at 7 days). Random forests significantly outperformed logistic regression in every comparison. Recalibration improved performance as much as ninefold – clinical recommendations with poorly calibrated predictions can lead to decision errors. Conclusions Machine learning on longitudinal clinical data may provide a scalable approach to broaden screening for risk of nonfatal suicide attempts in adolescents.

sample_claims.text: The recalibrated suicide-attempt risk model's predicted probabilities match observed attempt rates across risk deciles in held-out records, with calibration slope and intercept within pre-agreed bounds.

Within each band of predicted claim probability, the average prediction on a later, held-out year of policies is within the tolerance in the pricing policy of the observed claim rate, so no band of policyholders systematically subsidises another.

The fraud probabilities shown to analysts were recalibrated on more than 10,000 labelled past cases and agree with observed fraud rates on held-out cases, and the reliability diagram is published alongside the review tool.

techniques.name: Scenario-Based Simulation Testing
techniques.description: Scenario-based simulation testing checks an automated system, most often an automated driving system, by running it through a planned set of situations in a simulator and judging each run against criteria fixed in advance. Scenarios are written at three levels of detail: a functional scenario describes a situation in words (a car cuts in ahead on a motorway), a logical scenario turns it into parameters with ranges (speeds, gaps, road friction), and a concrete scenario fixes one value for every parameter so that the run can be reproduced exactly. Functional scenarios are derived from hazard analysis and from the operational design domain (the conditions the system is designed to work in), and concrete scenarios are sampled from the logical ranges, either to cover the whole range or to seek out rare, critical combinations, or are reconstructed from recorded incidents. Each concrete scenario is executed with the system under test in the loop, and pass or fail is decided against its expected behaviour, such as no collision, or by criticality measures such as time-to-collision, giving a record of which situations the system handles and which it does not. ISO 34502 gives a scenario-based safety evaluation framework of this kind for automated driving systems on limited-access highways.

example_use_cases.description: A developer of a motorway driving function derives cut-in, cut-out and stopped-vehicle scenarios from its hazard analysis, gives each logical scenario ranges for speeds, gaps and road friction, and runs several thousand sampled concrete scenarios in simulation for every software release, holding back any release in which a run ends in a collision the function was required to avoid.

A robotaxi operator rebuilds the fatal crashes recorded over a decade in the city where it operates as concrete simulation scenarios, and replays each one with its driving system in place of first one human driver and then the other, so that it can show regulators how the system behaves in the crash types that actually occur in its operating area.

An operator of an autonomous passenger ferry tests its collision-avoidance planner on head-on, crossing and overtaking encounters described in the international collision regulations, varying the other vessel's speed, bearing and visibility in a ship simulator, and checks in every run that the ferry keeps its required passing distance and makes the manoeuvre the regulations call for.

limitations.description: The evidence covers only the scenarios that were specified. Real operating conditions cannot be listed exhaustively, so a clean result shows that the system handles the catalogue, not that it is safe; the safety argument depends on how completely the functional scenarios were derived from the hazard analysis and operational design domain, which needs independent review.

Results are only as credible as the simulation. If the models of sensors, vehicle dynamics or other road users have not been validated against the real world, a system can pass in simulation and fail in operation, so key scenarios should be repeated on a test track or against recorded real data.

How concrete scenarios are sampled shapes what the results mean. Covering whole parameter ranges ignores how often each situation occurs, and searching for critical corner cases finds failures efficiently but over-represents rare situations, so neither supports a statement about real-world accident rates unless results are weighted by how often scenarios occur.

Pass criteria encode a judgement about acceptable behaviour. 'No collision' misses near misses and lucky escapes, while criticality measures such as time-to-collision need thresholds that the developer must choose and justify, and the verdicts change with them.

Building scenario catalogues, simulation environments and behaviour models for other road users takes specialist effort and substantial computing. ISO 34502 applies only to limited-access highways, so for urban roads, ships and other domains the scenario structure, pass criteria and coverage argument have to be built without the standard's support.

resources.title: Scenarios for Development, Test and Validation of Automated Vehicles
resources.abstract: The latest version of the ISO 26262 standard from 2016 represents the state of the art for a safety-guided development of safety-critical electric/electronic vehicle systems. These vehicle systems include advanced driver assistance systems and vehicle guidance systems. The development process proposed in the ISO 26262 standard is based upon multiple V-models, and defines activities and work products for each process step. In many of these process steps, scenario based approaches can be applied to achieve the defined work products for the development of automated driving functions. To accomplish the work products of different process steps, scenarios have to focus on various aspects like a human understandable notation or a description via state variables. This leads to contradictory requirements regarding the level of detail and way of notation for the representation of scenarios. In this paper, the authors discuss requirements for the representation of scenarios in different process steps defined by the ISO 26262 standard, propose a consistent terminology based on prior publications for the identified levels of abstraction, and demonstrate how scenarios can be systematically evolved along the phases of the development process outlined in the ISO 26262 standard.

resources.title: Create a new scenario tutorial — ScenarioRunner
Waymo simulated driving behavior in reconstructed fatal crashes within an autonomous vehicle operating domain
resources.abstract: Preventing and mitigating high severity collisions is one of the main opportunities for Automated Driving Systems (ADS) to improve road safety. This study evaluated the Waymo Driver's performance within real-world fatal collision scenarios that occurred in a specific operational design domain (ODD). To address the rare nature of high-severity collisions, this paper describes the addition of novel techniques to established safety impact assessment methodologies. A census of fatal, human-involved collisions was examined for years 2008 through 2017 for Chandler, AZ, which overlaps the current geographic ODD of the Waymo One fully automated ride-hailing service. Crash reconstructions were performed on all available fatal collisions that involved a passenger vehicle as one of the first collision partners and an available map in this ODD to determine the pre-impact kinematics of the vehicles involved in the original crashes. The final dataset consisted of a total of 72 crashes and 91 vehicle actors (52 initiators and 39 responders) for simulations. Next, a novel counterfactual "what-if'' simulation method was developed to synthetically replace human-driven crash participants one at a time with the Waymo Driver. This study focused on the Waymo Driver's performance when replacing one of the first two collision partners. The results of these simulations showed that the Waymo Driver was successful in avoiding all collisions when replacing the crash initiator, that is, the road user who made the initial, unexpected maneuver leading to a collision. Replacing the driver reacting (the responder) to the actions of the crash initiator with the Waymo Driver resulted in an estimated 82% of simulations where a collision was prevented and an additional 10% of simulations where the collision severity was mitigated (reduction in crash-level serious injury risk). The remaining 8% of simulations with the Waymo Driver in the responder role had a similar outcome to the original collision. All of these "unchanged" collisions involved both the original vehicle and the Waymo Driver being struck in the rear in a front-to-rear configuration. These results demonstrate the potential of fully automated driving systems to improve traffic safety compared to the performance of the humans originally involved in the collisions. The findings also highlight the major importance of driving behaviors that prevent entering a conflict situation (e.g. maintaining safe time gaps and not surprising other road users). However, methodological challenges in performing single instance counterfactual simulations based solely on police report data and uncertainty in ADS performance may result in variable performance, requiring additional analysis and supplemental methodologies. This study's methods provide insights on rare, severe events that would otherwise only be experienced after operating in extreme real-world driving distances (many billions of driving miles).

sample_claims.text: The motorway driving function passed every concrete scenario sampled from the cut-in, cut-out and stopped-vehicle logical scenarios derived from the hazard analysis, with no collisions and minimum time-to-collision above the agreed threshold.

In simulated reconstructions of the fatal crashes recorded in its operating area, the driving system avoided every crash in which it replaced the driver who initiated the conflict, and the crashes it did not avoid when replacing the responding driver are reported with their causes.
The ferry's collision-avoidance planner kept the required passing distance in every simulated head-on, crossing and overtaking encounter across the specified ranges of speed, bearing and visibility.
The scenario catalogue used for release testing covers every hazardous event identified in the hazard analysis and the full operational design domain, as confirmed by independent review.

techniques.name: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics
techniques.description: Bootstrap confidence intervals put a range around a model's measured performance, showing how much the score could differ had another test set of the same size been drawn from the same population. The labelled held-out evaluation set is resampled with replacement thousands of times, each resample holding as many cases as the original so that some cases appear more than once and others not at all, and the metric (an error rate, the area under a curve, a translation score) is recomputed on each resample from the model's stored predictions, with no retraining. The spread of these recomputed values stands in for the sampling distribution of the metric: the percentile interval takes its 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles for a 95 per cent interval, and the bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) interval shifts those percentiles to correct for bias and skew in that distribution. The statistic can also be the difference between two models scored on the same cases, recomputed on each shared resample, which shows whether an observed improvement is larger than the noise from test-set sampling. The result is the metric with lower and upper bounds at a stated confidence level, so a requirement such as a maximum false-positive rate can be checked against the bound rather than the point estimate.

example_use_cases.description: A medical-imaging company preparing a regulatory submission reports its fracture detector's sensitivity and specificity at the locked threshold with 95 per cent bootstrap intervals. Because each patient contributes several radiographs, it resamples patients rather than images, so the interval reflects the number of independent patients in the test set rather than the larger number of images.

A machine-translation team deciding whether to replace its production model scores the current and candidate systems on the same held-out sentences, recomputes the difference in BLEU score on 1,000 shared bootstrap resamples of those sentences, and approves the change only if the 95 per cent interval for the difference lies above zero.

A fisheries agency whose vessel-detection model must keep false alarms below 2 per cent of non-vessel image patches re-measures the false-positive rate each quarter on several thousand newly labelled patches, puts a bootstrap interval on it, and states compliance against the interval's upper bound. In a quarter where the labelled sample yields only a handful of false positives, the agency uses an exact binomial interval instead, because the bootstrap interval is too narrow at that count.

An evaluation team comparing two large language models on a 500-question internal benchmark reports each model's accuracy with a BCa bootstrap interval and puts a paired interval on the difference, which shows that a 1.5-point lead is within the sampling noise of a test set that size, so the team does not cite it as evidence that one model is better.

limitations.description: For a rate built from rare errors, such as a low false-positive rate, the interval is too narrow when the test set holds only a handful of errors. With 200 negatives and a true rate of 0.5 per cent, about a third of test sets have no false positives; the percentile interval is then [0, 0] and BCa may return no value. For a single proportion the exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) interval avoids this; the bootstrap earns its place on metrics with no simple formula.

Resampling single cases assumes they are independent. When several test cases come from one patient, vessel, user or time window, their errors are correlated, and resampling cases treats them as separate evidence, giving intervals that can be much too narrow. Resampling whole clusters (patients, days) instead restores the right width when there are enough clusters, which needs the cluster of each case to be recorded in the test set; with few clusters the interval is again too narrow.

The interval reflects only which cases happened to be in the test set. It says nothing about variation from retraining the model on other data or with another random seed, nor about whether the test set represents the deployment population, so a narrow interval on an unrepresentative test set is precise and still wrong. Uncertainty in a single prediction, from retraining on resampled training data, is a different procedure; see Bootstrap Ensembles.

If the decision threshold, the model or the metric was chosen by looking at the same test set, resampling that set leaves the interval centred on an optimistic estimate, because the selection effect is not reproduced in the resamples. The choice has to be made on data separate from the set that is resampled.

Coverage is approximate and improves with test-set size. Percentile intervals can be too narrow on small test sets, and more so for skewed metrics; the BCa interval corrects for bias and skew but not for the narrowness that comes from a small test set, so small test sets stay a problem. BCa also needs an extra leave-one-out pass over the test set, which is slow for large sets or costly metrics, and it returns no interval when every resample gives the same value.

resources.title: Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife
resources.abstract: We discuss the following problem: given a random sample X = (X1, X2, …, Xn) from an unknown probability distribution F, estimate the sampling distribution of some prespecified random variable R(X, F), on the basis of the observed data x. (Standard jackknife theory gives an approximate mean and variance in the case R(X, F) = θ(F̂) − θ(F), θ some parameter of interest.) A general method, called the "bootstrap," is introduced, and shown to work satisfactorily on a variety of estimation problems. The jackknife is shown to be a linear approximation method for the bootstrap. The exposition proceeds by a series of examples: variance of the sample median, error rates in a linear discriminant analysis, ratio estimation, estimating regression parameters, etc.

resources.title: Better Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
resources.abstract: We consider the problem of setting approximate confidence intervals for a single parameter θ in a multiparameter family. The standard approximate intervals based on maximum likelihood theory, , can be quite misleading. In practice, tricks based on transformations, bias corrections, and so forth, are often used to improve their accuracy. The bootstrap confidence intervals discussed in this article automatically incorporate such tricks without requiring the statistician to think them through for each new application, at the price of a considerable increase in computational effort. The new intervals incorporate an improvement over previously suggested methods, which results in second-order correctness in a wide variety of problems. In addition to parametric families, bootstrap intervals are also developed for nonparametric situations.

techniques.name: Operating-Point ROC Analysis
techniques.description: Operating-point ROC analysis measures how often a classifier makes each kind of mistake at the decision threshold it will actually use, which is the evidence behind claims such as 'the false-positive rate stays within acceptable bounds'. A classifier that outputs a score is turned into a yes-or-no decision by a threshold, and moving the threshold trades one kind of error against the other. On a labelled held-out set, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots the true-positive rate (the share of actual positives that are flagged, also called sensitivity) against the false-positive rate (the share of actual negatives wrongly flagged, equal to one minus specificity) at every possible threshold; the operating threshold is then chosen from the curve to meet a stated limit on one error rate or to minimise the expected cost of errors, or an existing threshold is confirmed. At that one threshold the analysis reports the confusion matrix (the counts of true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives) and the false-positive and false-negative rates with their complements, specificity and sensitivity. The output is a set of error rates tied to a named threshold and a named test set, against which a requirement on error rates can be checked.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's clinical informatics team evaluating a vendor's sepsis alert scores a year of its own admissions, plots the ROC curve and fixes the alert threshold its operations committee chose from the vendor's recommended range. At that threshold it reports sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and the share of all admissions that would trigger an alert, and uses the false-positive count and alert volume to decide whether ward staff can act on the alerts.

A card-payments company re-runs the analysis every month on transactions its fraud analysts have labelled, confirms that the false-positive rate at the live threshold is still under the limit agreed with its customer-service team, and, whenever the rate has drifted above that limit, reopens the threshold choice on the latest ROC curve and confirms the new threshold on the following month's labelled sample.

A manufacturer's quality engineers choose the threshold for a visual-inspection model by weighing the cost of scrapping a good part against the cost of shipping a defective one, using the ROC curve and the line's defect rate, then report the false-reject and defect-escape rates that the chosen threshold gives on a separate held-out production batch.

A rail operator's safety team assessing a camera-based obstacle detector for level crossings sets the decision threshold on a tuning set so that the miss rate meets the requirement allocated to the detector. It then measures the false-negative rate at that threshold on a separate set of recorded crossings, broken down into daylight, night and rain, and enters the confusion matrices in the safety case as verification evidence.

limitations.description: The rates are evidence only if they are measured on labelled cases that played no part in choosing the threshold. A threshold set to give a 1 per cent false-positive rate on a tuning set gives exactly that rate there by construction, and with a few hundred negative tuning cases its true rate on new data can be half as high again. Choosing the threshold on one set and reporting rates on another, or nesting the choice inside cross-validation, avoids this at the cost of more labelled data.

False-positive and true-positive rates do not change with how common the positive class is, but the share of alerts that are correct does. A false-positive rate within its limit can still mean most alerts are false when the condition is rare: at 90 per cent sensitivity and a 5 per cent false-positive rate, only about 15 per cent of alerts are correct when 1 case in 100 is positive. Claims about alert burden need the positive predictive value at the deployment prevalence as well.

A rate from a finite test set is an estimate, and with few negatives or few errors it can fall well below the true rate by chance. A claim that a rate is within a limit needs a confidence interval (exact binomial for a single rate; see Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics for other metrics) narrower than the margin to the limit. With no misses, about 3,000 positives show a miss rate below 1 in 1,000, and 30,000 below 1 in 10,000, at 95 per cent confidence.

The threshold is a fixed score, so the rates hold only while the scores for each class stay as in the test set. A new scanner, fraud pattern or patient mix shifts the scores and moves the false-positive rate with no change to the model, so the analysis must be repeated on labelled operational samples, which can be slow or costly. Labels matter too: where only flagged cases are reviewed, the rate for unflagged cases is unknown unless a random sample of them is labelled.

A single rate averages over the whole test set. It can meet its limit overall while exceeding it for a group of people or an operating condition (night-time images, one hospital site) that is rare in the test data. Rates need reporting for each group and condition the claim covers, each with enough cases to be informative, which can multiply the labelled data required.

resources.title: External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients
resources.abstract: Importance: The Epic Sepsis Model (ESM), a proprietary sepsis prediction model, is implemented at hundreds of US hospitals. The ESM's ability to identify patients with sepsis has not been adequately evaluated despite widespread use. Objective: To externally validate the ESM in the prediction of sepsis and evaluate its potential clinical value compared with usual care. Design, Setting, and Participants: This retrospective cohort study was conducted among 27 697 patients aged 18 years or older admitted to Michigan Medicine, the academic health system of the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, with 38 455 hospitalizations between December 6, 2018, and October 20, 2019. Exposure: The ESM score, calculated every 15 minutes. Main Outcomes and Measures: Sepsis, as defined by a composite of (1) the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention surveillance criteria and (2) International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision diagnostic codes accompanied by 2 systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria and 1 organ dysfunction criterion within 6 hours of one another. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve at the hospitalization level and with prediction horizons of 4, 8, 12, and 24 hours. Model calibration was evaluated with calibration plots. The potential clinical benefit associated with the ESM was assessed by evaluating the added benefit of the ESM score compared with contemporary clinical practice (based on timely administration of antibiotics). Alert fatigue was evaluated by comparing the clinical value of different alerting strategies. Results: We identified 27 697 patients who had 38 455 hospitalizations (21 904 women [57%]; median age, 56 years [interquartile range, 35-69 years]) meeting inclusion criteria, of whom sepsis occurred in 2552 (7%). The ESM had a hospitalization-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.63 (95% CI, 0.62-0.64). The ESM identified 183 of 2552 patients with sepsis (7%) who did not receive timely administration of antibiotics, highlighting the low sensitivity of the ESM in comparison with contemporary clinical practice. The ESM also did not identify 1709 patients with sepsis (67%) despite generating alerts for an ESM score of 6 or higher for 6971 of all 38 455 hospitalized patients (18%), thus creating a large burden of alert fatigue. Conclusions and Relevance: This external validation cohort study suggests that the ESM has poor discrimination and calibration in predicting the onset of sepsis. The widespread adoption of the ESM despite its poor performance raises fundamental concerns about sepsis management on a national level.

techniques.name: CycloneDX Machine Learning Bill of Materials
techniques.description: A CycloneDX ML-BOM (machine-learning bill of materials) is a machine-readable inventory of what a model is made of, written in the CycloneDX standard (ECMA-424) so that tools as well as people can check it. It applies the software bill of materials, a structured list of the components in a piece of software, to models: the model is declared as a component of type machine-learning-model with its identifiers, version, supplier, licence and file hashes, together with the base models it was derived from (its pedigree), the datasets used to train and evaluate it with their source, classification and owners, the libraries it depends on, and an optional structured model card giving its task, architecture, performance metrics, intended uses and known limitations. The BOM is written at release, by hand or with a generator that reads the model's repository and metadata, checked against the CycloneDX schema, and can be signed. Consumers then query it, for example to find every deployed model that uses a dataset or library found to be compromised, or to check a supplier's declared datasets and licences before purchase. Unlike a model card or datasheet, written for people to read, or an experiment log or data version history, which stay with the team that built the model, it is a parts list in a fixed schema that travels with the model and can be matched against vulnerability records and file hashes, but it records what its author declares and verifies none of it.

example_use_cases.description: A bank keeps an ML-BOM for every deployed model, recording each base model by its Hugging Face package URL and revision, the fine-tuning datasets, the framework libraries and the file hashes. When a compromised base-model release or a vulnerability in a model-loading library is announced, its security team queries the BOMs to list the affected deployments within hours and decides which to withdraw or patch.

A hospital trust buying a diagnostic imaging model requires the supplier to deliver a signed ML-BOM with each version. Before the model enters clinical evaluation, the acceptance team checks the BOM's signature, compares its file hashes with the delivered files and checks the listed libraries against known-vulnerability records.

A government department procuring a document-classification model asks bidders for an ML-BOM whose model-card and dataset fields declare each training and evaluation dataset with its source, licence and owner, and the model's known technical limitations. Its assessors and later its auditors read and query these declarations to compare bids and to check what the chosen supplier said it used.

A software company generates an ML-BOM for each release of its customer-support assistant with an open-source generator, recording the base and embedding models, the quantised model file and the framework libraries with hashes. Its security team compares each new BOM with the previous release's to catch an unreviewed change of base model or library before the release ships.

limitations.description: It records what its author declares. Nothing in the format checks that the listed datasets were the ones used, that the model-card fields are true or that the list is complete, so a BOM is evidence that a disclosure was made, not that it is accurate. Hashes and a signature show that the document and the files it lists have not changed since it was written, which is a different thing.

Almost every field is optional: ECMA-424 requires a component's type and name and little else, so a BOM can pass schema validation while saying almost nothing. In a 2026 preprint that generated ML-BOMs with one open-source tool for about 98,000 Hugging Face models, every BOM had the required fields, but only 39% named a dataset, 17% listed technical limitations and 0.2% had a meaningful description. A claim needs the fields it relies on to be checked, not only schema validity.

Generators can fill only what they can read: hub metadata, model-card text and configuration files. Training data, fine-tuning history and settings that the publisher never wrote down stay empty, and for a model bought from a supplier the BOM is only as complete as the supplier chooses to make it.

Each BOM describes one version of one model. Fine-tuning, quantisation, a new framework release or a changed dataset needs a new BOM, and the ability to answer 'which of our models use this component?' when a compromise is disclosed depends on BOMs being regenerated and kept for every deployed version, which is a standing process cost rather than a one-off task.

techniques.name: Malicious Model-File Scanning
techniques.description: Malicious model-file scanning checks a downloaded or received model file for code that would run when the file is loaded, without loading it. Several common ways of saving (serialising) models can carry such code, above all Python's pickle format, the default for PyTorch checkpoints and the usual format for scikit-learn models, whose files can instruct the loader to import and call any Python function, so that loading an untrusted file can hand an attacker control of the machine; since version 2.6 PyTorch's own loader by default allows only a small set of known-safe functions, but some libraries switch that off to load their models. The named method is ModelScan, an open-source scanner from Protect AI, which chooses a check by file extension and reads the file as data: for pickle-based files it lists the functions the file would import and compares them with a graded list of unsafe ones, such as the os, subprocess and socket modules and Python's built-in eval and exec, and for Keras and TensorFlow files it flags Lambda layers, which hold arbitrary Python, and operations that read or write files. It reports each finding with a severity from critical to low and exits with a non-zero code when it finds any, so a pipeline can stop the file before anything loads it. The evidence is a record that no listed unsafe call was found in the files scanned; unlike data-poisoning detection it examines the saved file rather than the training data, and it shows neither that the file is safe, nor how the model behaves, nor who produced the file.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's machine-learning platform team adds a ModelScan step to the job that imports models from public hubs into its internal registry. A critical or high-severity finding stops the import and opens a ticket for the security team, which decides whether the third-party checkpoint may enter the registry at all.

A university's research-computing service scans every checkpoint users upload to shared GPU storage, including PyTorch .pt files and scikit-learn models saved with joblib, before jobs on nodes shared between research groups can load them, and quarantines any file with a critical finding until its owner explains the flagged imports.

A manufacturer's operational-technology security team scans each Keras visual-inspection model delivered by an outside contractor before it is copied to factory edge devices. A flagged Lambda layer is accepted only after the contractor supplies the layer's source code and an engineer confirms that it does nothing beyond resizing and normalising images.

limitations.description: It finds only what is on its list. In a peer-reviewed comparison ModelScan missed 9 of 84 known malicious models: five called functions not on its list (the authors' own example wrote files through Python's pathlib module instead of open), three loaded a further payload at run time, for example through numpy.load, and one hid its payload after an early stop instruction, where the scanner stopped reading. A clean scan shows that no known pattern was found, not that the file is safe.

Attackers adapt faster than the list. A peer-reviewed study (2026) found 22 routes by which five frameworks load pickled data, 19 of which evaded all four scanners it tested, ModelScan included, and in a 2026 preprint ModelScan detected none of 3,000 new attack files. A scan is only as current as the scanner release and unsafe list it ran with.

It checks only the files and formats it recognises, chosen by file extension, and skips the rest, so a pass can cover only some of what the loader will open. Showing that a model was checked needs the list of skipped files (ModelScan can print it) and a check that every file the loading code reads was among those scanned.

Findings need judgement. Every Keras Lambda layer is flagged, though Lambda layers are meant for ordinary pre- and post-processing, and benign models from some libraries import functions that pickle scanners treat as suspicious (one peer-reviewed study describes a widely downloaded model flagged this way). Someone able to read the flagged imports or layer code, or to question the model's author, has to decide each case.

It looks for code that runs on load, not for harmful behaviour in the weights. A model whose weights were altered to carry a backdoor, or that was trained on poisoned data, contains no unsafe call and scans clean, as does any file in a format that cannot hold code, such as safetensors; ModelScan's own documentation notes that weights can be manipulated in such formats. Backdoor and poisoning checks are separate techniques.

techniques.name: Model Signing
techniques.description: Model signing lets the publisher of a machine-learning model attach a cryptographic signature to the model's files, so that anyone who later loads them can check who released them and that no file has changed since. Under the Open Source Security Foundation's Model Signing (OMS) specification and its reference tool, model-signing, the publisher computes a hash (a short fingerprint that changes if a single byte of the file changes) of every file in the model directory, such as weights, configuration, tokeniser and any dataset files kept with them, lists the hashes in a sorted manifest and signs the manifest, producing a detached signature file kept beside the model. The signature can be made with the publisher's own key, with a certificate from an organisation's certificate authority, or through Sigstore, which issues a short-lived certificate tied to a verified online identity, such as a person's account or a build pipeline's, and records each signing event in a transparency log, an append-only record that can be inspected afterwards. Before loading, the consumer verifies the signature against the signer it expects, recomputes every hash and rejects the model if any listed file differs or is missing or, unless that check is switched off, an unlisted file has appeared, so the evidence is a pass or fail tied to a named signer and an exact set of files. Unlike the unsigned file hashes kept by data-versioning tools, it shows who stands behind the files, and unlike a watermark, which is trained into the weights so that it survives in an altered copy, it is broken by any change; it says nothing about how the model behaves or what it was trained on.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's machine-learning platform team signs each model at the end of its training pipeline, using the pipeline's own workload identity through Sigstore, and configures its model-serving cluster to load only models whose signature verifies against that identity. Its security team watches the transparency log for signing events under that identity that match no approved release, to decide whether a model reached production outside the release process.

A vehicle maker's perception team downloads a pretrained object detector from a supplier catalogue that signs every model it publishes. Before fine-tuning, it verifies the download against the supplier's published certificate and files the verification output in its supplier-acceptance record, so later reviews can show exactly which files the work started from.

A hospital's imaging department receives quarterly updates to a vendor's chest X-ray triage model. Its clinical engineering team verifies each update against the vendor's certificate and rejects any update whose signature fails, or that contains a file the signature does not cover, before it enters the clinical validation environment.

A public research institute releases an open model together with the test set behind its published benchmark, signing both in one bundle, so that a laboratory re-running the benchmark can confirm that the weights and the test data are byte for byte the ones the institute released before comparing its results with the published ones.

limitations.description: It shows who released the files and that they have not changed, nothing more. A model carrying a malicious pickle payload, a backdoor or the effects of poisoned training data verifies perfectly if its publisher signed it, whether through carelessness or because the publisher's own pipeline was compromised before signing. The originating paper states that signing tells the user nothing about what a model does or how it was produced, so content checks are still needed.

A valid signature is only as good as the consumer's check of who made it. A model signed with an attacker's own identity, or by an account named to look like a well-known organisation (a documented attack on model hubs), verifies cleanly unless the verifier insists on the specific identity, certificate or public key it expects. Consumers need a maintained list of trusted signers for each model source.

A stolen signing key, or a compromised account at the identity provider used for Sigstore signing, produces valid signatures. With Sigstore every signature is recorded in a transparency log, so a publisher that monitors the log for its own identity can spot signatures it did not make; with the key and certificate methods the specification does not require a log entry, so misuse of a key may go unnoticed.

Any change to the files breaks verification, including legitimate ones such as quantisation, conversion to another file format or adding a file. Each derived model needs a new signature from whoever produced it, and that signature says nothing about how the derivative relates to the signed original; recording that relationship needs a separate provenance record, such as the pedigree section of an ML-BOM.

It protects only where verification is enforced. Most models on public hubs are unsigned (fewer than 2% of Hugging Face models used the hub's GPG commit-signing option, per studies the originating paper cites), and an unchecked signature protects nobody. Verification re-hashes every file, and hashing dominates the cost: a 1 TB file took about 13 minutes on a 128-vCPU server in the originating paper's benchmark, which matters if very large models are verified at every load.

resources.title: Position: Machine Learning Models Have a Supply Chain Problem
resources.abstract: Powerful machine learning (ML) models are now readily available online, which creates exciting possibilities for users who lack the deep technical expertise or substantial computing resources needed to develop them. On the other hand, this type of open ecosystem comes with many risks. In this paper, we argue that the current ecosystem for open ML models contains significant supply-chain risks, some of which have been exploited already in real attacks. These include an attacker replacing a model with something malicious (e.g., malware), or a model being trained using a vulnerable version of a framework or on restricted or poisoned data. We then explore how Sigstore, a solution designed to bring transparency to open-source software supply chains, can be used to bring transparency to open ML models, in terms of enabling model publishers to sign their models and prove properties about the datasets they use.

techniques.name: STRIDE-AI Threat Modelling
techniques.description: STRIDE-AI is a threat-modelling method for machine-learning (ML) systems, proposed by Mauri and Damiani (2021, extended 2022), that lists, before any testing, the ways an attacker could compromise each asset of an ML pipeline and how serious each would be. It adapts Microsoft's STRIDE scheme, in which each of six threat types (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege) breaks one security property (authenticity, integrity, non-repudiation, confidentiality, availability and authorisation), and gives each property an ML-specific definition: confidentiality, for example, means that querying a model reveals nothing beyond its inputs and outputs. The analyst surveys the assets produced across the ML life cycle, such as raw, labelled and validation data, hyperparameters, trained and deployed models and the model architecture, and with each asset's owners runs a failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA, a structured review of how a component could fail and with what effect), answering set questions about how the asset could fail, be misused or be abused. Each failure mode is mapped to the properties it would break and so to STRIDE threats, using the method's published tables of asset types, properties and known attacks; the analyst then works with developers to draw threat trees showing the conditions under which each threat could be realised, and rates each threat's priority (the worked example uses DREAD, which scores five factors from 1 to 10). The output is a threat model, a table of assets, threatened properties, threats and priorities with their threat trees: the method attacks and measures nothing, and choosing and testing controls for the threats it finds is left to other techniques.

example_use_cases.description: The security architect for a solar-farm operator's fault-prediction service, which trains on sensor readings streamed from plant data loggers to an external ML platform, maps each asset to its threatened properties. The threat trees show that the loggers' signatures stop injected readings but not label flipping, because labels are added later on the operator's own platform, so that threat is ranked and passed to the platform team.

Before buying a third-party chest X-ray triage model, a hospital's information-security team runs STRIDE-AI over the vendor's pipeline documentation: training data, the supplied model file, the inference service and the results sent to radiologists. Threats such as tampering with the model file and disclosure of training images through model outputs set the scope of the security tests and contract terms the hospital asks the vendor to meet.

A bank's model-security lead repeats the analysis when a card-fraud model moves from monthly retraining to online learning on live transactions. The transaction stream becomes a training-data asset that anyone making transactions can influence, so tampering with it to drift the model is added as a threat, rated and entered in the bank's risk register.

limitations.description: A finished threat model is not evidence that no other threats exist. Its coverage depends on the asset survey and on what the analysts know; the authors state that ML vulnerabilities cannot be fully enumerated in one pass and that failure modes must be updated as the system and known attacks change, and a 2006 Microsoft account of STRIDE notes there is no well-established way to measure a threat model's quality. Claims should state what was in scope and when the analysis was last revised.

STRIDE-AI identifies and ranks threats but does not choose or test controls. Both papers' abstracts say it guides control selection, but neither gives a procedure: the 2021 paper puts control selection outside its scope and the 2022 paper leaves it to future work, noting that no security control framework designed for ML was available. A claim that the threats are mitigated needs separate evidence, such as attack tests against each control and a control catalogue taken from another source.

Priorities are expert judgements. The worked example uses DREAD scores, which the authors note can give inconsistent results between raters and are no longer recommended as the only basis for ranking. Two teams may rank the same threats differently, so claims that rest on the ranking are stronger when several people score independently or a published severity scale such as a bug bar is used.

The mapping from failure modes to properties and threats is done by hand for every asset, and needs asset owners, developers and a security analyst together. Later work describes it as lacking automation, which limits how far it scales to large pipelines; each significant change, such as moving a model to online learning, means repeating part of the analysis.

The published catalogue of assets, failure modes and known attacks was built in 2021-22 around the life cycle of a conventionally trained model, from requirements to maintenance. It does not list assets specific to language-model applications and agents, such as system prompts, retrieval corpora or connected tools, so analysts of those systems must add the assets and their threats themselves, without guidance from the method.
